credits.readme:
Maria Sibylla Merian, *Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium*, plate 9
(pomegranate with blue morpho), engraved by Joseph Mulder, Amsterdam 1705,
hand-coloured. Smithsonian Libraries copy, digitised for the Biodiversity
Heritage Library (Internet Archive `Metamorphosisin00Meri`). Public domain.
The separation is ours. No third-party code.

files.text:
In June 1699 Maria Sibylla Merian, fifty-two years old, sailed from Amsterdam for Surinam with her younger daughter, Dorothea Maria. She had sold most of her paintings and her collection to pay for the passage. For years she had looked at the insects of that colony in the cabinets of Amsterdam collectors, pinned in rows or floating in jars of spirits, beautiful and dead, with nothing to say what they had eaten or what they had been before. She had spent her life, since she was a girl in Frankfurt keeping silkworms, on exactly that question: what a caterpillar becomes, and on what plant.

They took rooms in Paramaribo, at the mouth of the river, and went upriver to the plantations when they could. Merian kept caterpillars in boxes in the house, fed each on the leaves she had found it on, and wrote down the day it stopped eating, the day it spun or hardened, the day something came out and opened its wings. She painted them on vellum in watercolour with their plant beside them, egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and moth or butterfly on one branch, so that a single sheet held a whole life. She did not do it alone. Indigenous and enslaved African people cut the paths, brought her what they found and told her what the plants were for, and some of what they told her went into her book. In the summer of 1701 the heat and a fever sent her home.

In Amsterdam the watercolours went to three engravers, Joseph Mulder, Pieter Sluyter and Daniel Stoopendaal, who cut them into sixty copper plates. This one is Mulder’s; his name is in the margin under the branch. The plates were inked and printed on large sheets of good paper, and in 1705 the book came out in Latin and in Dutch. A buyer could take it plain, line alone on cream paper, or pay a good deal more to have every plate coloured by hand.

The colouring was done in Merian’s house, by Merian and her daughters, from painted models kept as patterns, so that each copy of a butterfly came out the same blue. It was thin watercolour bound with gum arabic, laid one colour at a time: flat washes brushed up to the engraved line, which held them, and now and then a little over it. The engraver had already done the shading in hatching; the wash only had to give the colour, and the line showed through. Watercolour goes on dark and glossy and dries paler and dull, with the pigment drawn to the rim as the water leaves, and a colourist learned to lay each wash a shade stronger than it was meant to end.

On this sheet a pomegranate splits open under a branch in flower, a pale striped caterpillar along one twig and a chrysalis lying across the fruit. Above them is the morpho twice. Closed, from below, it is brown and eyed like a dry leaf, which is how it rests; open, from above, it is the blue it shows only in flight, the colour the whole page waits for.

A coloured copy cost forty-five guilders or more, more than a skilled worker in Amsterdam earned in two months, and Merian sold them from her house. After her death in 1717 Dorothea sold the copper plates to a publisher, and the book went on being printed, and coloured by other hands, for most of the century. No two copies are quite alike. Put two side by side and the leaves are greener in one and the fruit rosier in the other; a wash runs over the line here and stops short of it there: the hand of whoever sat at the table that day, matching the model as well as they could, waiting for each colour to dry before laying the next.

# hand-colouring A plate from Maria Sibylla Merian's *Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium* (Amsterdam, 1705) coloured by hand as you read. It arrives as the bare engraving, black-brown line on its own cream paper, the way uncoloured copies were sold. As you scroll, washes of watercolour go down one area at a time: the leaves and stems first, then the fruit and flowers, the caterpillar and chrysalis, the brown morpho underside, and the blue of the open morpho last. Each wash spreads as a wet front from where the brush went down, held back by the engraved lines; it is darker and faintly glossy while wet, dries from the edges inward with its pigment drawn to the rim and settling into the paper's tooth, and ends as exactly the real coloured plate. Scroll back and it un-colours. ```html
``` Or `import { handColouring } from './hand-colouring.js'` and call `handColouring(section, { src, mode, runway, webgl })`; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---------------|----------|----------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The plate's JSON (size, paper, the washes in painting order). Next to it: `.webp` (the coloured plate), `-bare.webp` (the uncoloured impression), `-flat.webp` (each wash blurred inside its area: the pigment in suspension) and `-map.webp` (lossless: wash index, arrival time, distance to edge, distance to a damp neighbour). | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned stage on a runway. `static`: the finished plate in the flow. | | `data-runway` | `runway` | `390` | Section height in svh. The schedule is laid out in svh of travel (big areas 12-20svh, the morpho's blue about 24svh per wing) and scaled to fit. | | `data-webgl` | `webgl` | `on` | `off` forces the 2D fallback (a plain cross-fade from bare to coloured). | Events (bubbling, for sound later): `hand-colouring:wash` with `detail: { index, kind }` each time a wash goes down while scrolling forward (kinds: `leaf`, `stem`, `fruit`, `flower`, `caterpillar`, `chrysalis`, `butterfly`, `morpho`, `morpho-blue`), and `hand-colouring:done` when the last wash is dry. ## The real thing What a colourist's wash does on a printed sheet (Curtis, Anderson, Seims, Fleischer and Salesin, *Computer-Generated Watercolor*, SIGGRAPH 1997; studies of 18th-century hand-coloured prints; Dill et al. 2021 on Merian's plates): - The brush carries a bead of thin, gum-bound watercolour. Water runs out ahead of the hairs; the wet front advances unevenly (the sizing is uneven), creeps along and is slowed by the raised ink of the engraved lines, and stops at the outline, now and then a little over it. - Wet paint is darker and more saturated than it will dry, and the film catches the light. - While wet the pigment is in suspension and the wash looks smooth. As the film thins, pigment settles into the paper's tooth (granulation), and capillary flow toward the pinned, fastest-drying edge carries pigment to the rim: a darker ring, a paler middle. Edges dry first. A dry wash is lighter and matte. - Where a wash is laid against one that is still damp, water runs back into the damp one: a bloom, a pale lobe with a dark frilled edge. - Merian's workshop coloured from painted models, one colour at a time. Modelled: all of the above, as transients that settle into the plate's own washes (which already carry their real rims, granulation and blooms). Simplified: one wash per area (no glazing in layers, no body colour or gum highlights laid separately); neighbouring leaves or petals are laid as one passage; two washes are usually wet at once (one spreading, one drying), so the eye can follow a brush; the order is by kind and climbs the plant from the cut branch upward, not a documented colourist's order. ## How it works **Offline (Python, scripts kept out of the component).** From the scan of the coloured plate: 1. *Line from colour.* In linear light, the least-absorbed channel of each pixel is compared with its local mean (a 3.5px Gaussian) and with its local ground (a 6px grey closing). A wash darkens all three alike and its hue darkens one channel only, so the ratio isolates the engraved strokes whatever colour lies under them. A smoothstep threshold gives a clean, anti-aliased line mask at full scan resolution, which is area-averaged to the output size. 2. *The uncoloured impression.* The paper under the washes is filled in from the surrounding paper (normalised convolution at two scales), and the line mask is inked in fresh copperplate ink, a warm black-brown `#2a221c` at full stroke, keeping the mask's anti-aliasing. Away from the washes the bare image is the scan itself, so the start and the end agree everywhere colour never was. 3. *Areas.* The line-free colour layer (a grey closing of the scan) is cut into SLIC superpixels inside the painted mask, merged on a region adjacency graph by Lab colour, thin pale fringes folded into neighbours, split into connected components, then merged again where two areas of the same kind meet across a border that is not an engraved line (a light and a dark half of one leaf), and into passages of neighbouring leaves or petals. Kinds come from colour and from boxes drawn round the insects. 45 washes. 4. *Arrival.* For each area a brush path runs along its principal axis from the upper end; the wet front's arrival time is the minimum over points on the path of (when the brush got there + geodesic travel time), with a speed field of low-frequency noise slowed by 75% on engraved lines (scikit-image `MCP_Geometric`). 5. The map holds per pixel the wash index (in painting order), the arrival time, the distance to the wash's edge and the distance to the border with a wash laid just before it. The outline zone just beyond each wash belongs to it and is reached last. **In the browser.** One quad, one fragment shader. A 256×1 state texture carries each wash's fill and drying progress, computed from scroll on the CPU. Per pixel: the wash transmittance is `coloured / bare`; while wet it is taken from the flat (blurred) wash, darkened (optical density × 1.5) and given a faint sheen; as it dries (edge first: drying threshold from distance to edge and arrival time) it moves to the real wash, with a transient rim `exp(-d/2.6px)`, a paler middle, granulation from a paper-tooth noise, and a bloom along a damp neighbour. When every wash is dry the shader computes `bare × (coloured / bare)`: the original plate, pixel for pixel. - Images are resampled to the canvas's pixel size on the CPU (high-quality smoothing), so the hatching never aliases and no mipmaps are needed. The map is uploaded once, exact, as an unpremultiplied ImageBitmap and sampled nearest. - Scroll is followed on a critically damped spring (quicker going back). - The canvas covers the pinned stage and draws the sheet itself (a sharp, anti-aliased trimmed edge and a tight shadow). On a narrow screen the sheet fills the width, and while it is being coloured the view zooms in (up to 1.75x, until the sheet nearly fills the height) and drifts after the washes that are wet: a camera path computed from the schedule and smoothed along the scroll, so it is a pure function of scroll position. It zooms back out to the whole sheet at the end. The pictures are packed at the zoomed size and mipmapped (WebGL2), so the zoomed-out sheet stays clean; with WebGL1 there is no zoom. - The map is lossless WebP saved with `exact` (no alpha-0 pixels), decoded as an unpremultiplied ImageBitmap, so the wash indices arrive intact. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---------------|--------------------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the page around the sheet | | `--hc-gutter` | `var(--gutter)` | side padding of the stage (the demo uses 5px on phones so the sheet fills the width) | | `--hc-runway` | set by the script | section height in scroll mode | The sheet keeps the plate's own paper: it is a page of a book, a trimmed sheet with a tight shadow, edge sharp. ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS the finished coloured plate stays as an ``; the canvas is `aria-hidden`. The art is ornament (`alt=""`); credits are in `assets/credits.json`. - Reduced motion: no runway, the finished coloured plate, still. - Phone: the plate fills the width; nothing is interactive, so a swipe always scrolls. ## Cost - Assets 3.1 MB: coloured 0.8 MB, bare 1.1 MB, flat 0.1 MB, map 1.1 MB (lossless), JSON 4 KB. - One full-screen quad, about a dozen texture reads per pixel inside washes, one inside untouched paper. A frame draws only while the scroll spring is moving and the section is on screen (IntersectionObserver); nothing runs when idle or in a hidden tab. DPR capped at 2. ## Making a new plate Scripts (in the builder's scratch folder): `s1_layers.py` (crop inside the sheet, white balance, wash layer, paper, painted mask), `s2_bare.py` (line mask, uncoloured impression, tinted-hatching areas), `s3_segment.py` (superpixels and colour merging), `s4_schedule.py` (folding, kinds, order, arrival fields, export). Each plate needs a small JSON of boxes round its insects and fruit. Look at the bare image and the area map at full size before exporting. ## Credits Maria Sibylla Merian, *Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium*, plate 9 (pomegranate with blue morpho), engraved by Joseph Mulder, Amsterdam 1705, hand-coloured. Smithsonian Libraries copy, digitised for the Biodiversity Heritage Library (Internet Archive `Metamorphosisin00Meri`). Public domain. The separation is ours. No third-party code.
